Overview
The story of the two men from Egulac is a Comanche creation myth that explains the origin of the moon. It is a part of the larger mythology of the Plains Indians, in which the moon is either a man or a woman who left the earth in a canoe that turned into the moon. The myths about the moon are accompanied by stories about the creation of the sun, the stars, and the planets. These celestial bodies were created when the earth was young and the Comanche people were just beginning to learn about the natural world.
The two men from Egulac are important Comanche heroes, much like the hero of another well-known Comanche myth, the myth of the creation of the sun. One night two men from Egulac went out hunting, and when they had gone a little way they saw a woman sitting in the middle of a circle of firelight. She was throwing chips of wood into the fire, and every chip she threw in, she would say, "One chip, one shot, one wound, one death." The two men watched her for a long time, and then they went back to their camp and told the other men what they had seen.
They went out and saw her again the next night, and the same thing happened. And the third night, they saw her again. This time, the youngest man said, "We can't let her keep talking like that. We must try to save her." So he took his gun and shot her, and when they got up in the morning they found that there were two dead men lying beside the woman's body.
They knew that the bullets they had used were made of lead, and that the woman had said, "One chip, one shot, one wound, one death." They knew that they were responsible for her death, and they felt very sorry about it. And from that time on, they never hunted in that place again.

When they come across a cabin, they enter and find a beautiful young woman, Mary Ellen Foster, who is accompanied by a crippled boy, Ralph.  Ralph is able to communicate only through writing, and it eventually emerges that he is mute.  Mary Ellen cooks the hunters a meal, and they spend the night in the cabin.  In the morning, the hunters set out to continue their hunt, and accidentally shoot and kill Mary Ellen's beloved cow.  When they discover that there is no road back to the cabin, they agree to leave Ralph with Mary Ellen and return to the town of Temescah to report the death of the cow and to try to find a road leading back to the cabin.  Upon reaching Temescah, the hunters learn that there has been a law passed that all mute persons must be given the opportunity to vote.  Ralph is of voting age, and therefore the town must provide him with a ballot and a box in which to deposit it.  The story ends with the observation that "there wasn't a dry eye in the house."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be killed by the spirits of the water.

Origins
This story comes from the Ojibwa/Anishinaabe people of North America. It is a part of a cycle of stories that explain the creation of the world and the rules of human behavior. The stories are taught through the use of allegories and metaphors, and are designed to be heard, not read.
The Egulac story is one of many that explain the dangers of being arrogant or mocking someone else's beliefs. It is also one of several stories that describe the consequences of not heeding warnings from elders.

Overview
The Egulac legend is a variation of the more general myth of two men. The men in this myth are usually presented as rivals, and one of them is often a trickster figure. The two men are usually engaged in some sort of contest, often a swimming contest, and usually one of them dies as a result. The myth has been analyzed as representing the conflict between individualism and community values.

Distribution
The Egulac legend is most commonly told in the northern Great Plains and in the Arctic, and it has been recorded among the Ojibwa, Dakota, Lakota, Cheyenne, and Aanápèe/Anápèe (a Shoshonean people). A variant of the myth with the main characters being Coyote and Crow has been recorded among the Yukon Hän and Aanápèe/Anápèe. The story of Egulac has also been adapted for children's books and has appeared on PBS's The Magic Door.

Description and plot outline
The story follows two traveling salesmen, George and Hank, who stay at the same inn while on their separate ways. The innkeeper, a cranberry farmer, tries to swindle the two travelers by selling them a worthless map to the "Canyon of the Soul" for $5,000. George pays the price but immediately suspects a scam; he enlists Hank to help him investigate the matter. After following the innkeeper to a secret location, George discovers that the "Canyon of the Soul" is in fact a quarry where the innkeeper mines and sells cranberries. George angrily demands his money back, and after a brief struggle, the innkeeper reveals that he only had $5,000 in the first place, and that the rest was a fraud. George and Hank agree to let the innkeeper keep the $5,000 and to leave the rest of the debt unpaid.

They paddled to the bank and saw a fire with three young women dancing around it. Two of the women were Native American and the third was a white woman. The men had never seen a white woman before. They approached the women, introduced themselves, and asked where they came from. The women said they were lost. The men offered the women shelter for the night, and after the women accepted, the men realized that they had no place for the women to sleep. They decided to share their blankets with the women. As they were trying to decide where to place the women, a bear came out of the woods and roared. The women screamed. The men reached for their guns, and after a moment of confusion, everyone calmed down. The men realized that the bear was not real, but a dream. They built a shelter for the women and slept on the ground near it. In the morning, the men asked the women if they wanted to go back to their village. The women said they did not know the way, and the men realized that they had dreamed the entire experience. They took the women back to their village and then returned home. From then on, the men went to the village often to visit the women.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". They escaped to the shore, hiding behind rocks, and then they saw a canoe with many warriors in it. And one of the men said to the other: "What shall we do? Let us hide here until they go away." The other man said: "No, let us go on board and try to fight them." So they went on board and fought them, and all the men in the canoe were killed, and they took their clothes off, and the two men swam to the shore again, and they were very cold. And when the sun rose they saw a man on the shore warming himself, and they went to him and asked him who he was, and he said he was a doctor of the people of Egulac and had been left behind to care for the sick. And they said: "We are the men who were in the canoe last night." The doctor said: "I see now that you are the men who were in the canoe last night, because you have torn your clothes and have become like sick people." Then the two men went away and told the people of Egulac what had happened. 
The people of Egulac were very angry when they heard this, and they sent a war-party to fight the people of the other side of the river. But the people on the other side of the river were much more powerful, and they killed many of the people of Egulac and took others prisoner. And the people of Egulac were very afraid. And from that time they never went down to the river to hunt seals anymore.

### Background

This story is one of several "turtle tales" that have been circulating among Native Americans in the northern United States and Canada for thousands of years. In this tale, a man dies as a result of his own foolishness or arrogance. The surviving spouse is often an innocent victim of the events, and there is a sense of the absurd or tragic in the way the couple communicates.

The answer is: , a Comanche tribe, stole two horses from a band of Yamparika Indians. The Yamparikas pursued the Egulac men for three days and nights, until they came to a mountain covered with rock formations, which was the boundary between their land and the land of the Wetumpka. The Egulac men had hidden the stolen horses in a canyon behind one of the rock formations. When the Yamparikas came to the mountain, they divided their forces, with half the tribe climbing the mountain to look for the horses, and the other half staying below to guard the trail.
After dark, the half of the Egulac tribe that was below the mountain began to sing songs and shout, pretending to be the Yamparikas, in an attempt to lure the guarding half away from the horses. At first, the Yamparikas did not take the bait, but after three nights of the same ruse, they were tricked, and two-thirds of the tribe was killed or captured. The remaining Yamparikas returned home, leaving the Egulac tribe to enjoy the stolen horses.
From then on, the rock formations were known as "the places where the horses were hidden" and "the places where the people were killed." The Egulac tribe told the story as a cautionary tale about the dangers of greed.

Source
Margaret Lewis, "One Night Two Men from Egulac," The Story of the Old West, p. 183.

Notes
This story is very similar to the story of the horse thieves in the 1930 Disney short, "Three Little Squirrels". The main differences are that in the Disney story, the horse thieves steal three horses, and they are caught by the owner, who rolls a boulder onto the thieves.

The answer is: , a comedic short story by Mark Twain, first published in The Niagara Book (1903), and collected in Twain's 1907 book My Debut as a Literary Person with Other Essays and Stories. The story was first published in book form in 1923 as One Night - Two Men - Mark Twain. It was one of the most popular of Twain's works during his lifetime.

Plot summary
The story follows Huckleberry Finn and Jim on their raft during the period just after the Civil War. They stop at a town where a dispute between two men, one white and one black, is pending. The black man, Tom Canaan, has stolen a mule from the white man, Simon Legree. Legree represents everything that is cruel and unjust in the world, and Canaan's theft is purely a matter of self-defense. Twain, through Huck, sympathizes completely with Canaan. The white man had seized Canaan and his family, threatening to sell them back into slavery in the South. Canaan had fought his way free, and in the course of the struggle, he grabbed Legree's mule and made his escape.
Legree represents the foolishness of trying to enforce slavery in the post-Civil War world: his attempt to re-enslave Canaan and his family ends in humiliation and defeat. The episode also shows the absurdity of attempting to maintain racial distinctions in a world where everyone is mixed with everyone else. Canaan is "white" enough to pass for a white man's son, and his son is "black" enough to be mistaken for a slave. In fact, the entire population of the town is interracially mixed. The "white" people are actually of mixed race, as are the "black" people. Everyone is of mixed race, and everyone knows it.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. After they had swum a while, one of them said to the other: "Do you know what I think about this water?" The other man asked him, "What do you mean? Do you mean about its being cold and dark and deep?"
"No," the first man said, "I mean about its being able to drown."
There was a pause while the other man considered this. Then he said, "What do you mean, it can drown?"
"Well," the first man explained, "you know how it is with this water, it's so deep you can't see the bottom. And if you swim down far enough, you'll see that the bottom is just as dark as the water above it. And if you swim down far enough, you'll find that the dark bottom is just as hard to reach as the surface is. And if you try to swim down even further, you'll find that the water is just as thick as the air above it. And if you try to swim down even further than that, who knows? Maybe the water stops altogether and there's nothing below it but the dark. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be killed by the spirits in the water.
The younger man laughed at his friend's superstition and dived into the river. As he was swimming, a creature resembling a large rubber tire came toward him. He climbed onto it and was carried downstream. He jumped off and was drowned in the shallow water at the edge of the channel.
The older man, who had watched his friend's death, said, "I told you so." As he was explaining to the young man's body how he had died, a second creature came toward him. He climbed onto it and was carried downstream for a short distance. He jumped off and was drowned in the shallow water at the edge of the channel.
The Egulac people believe that the two men in the story are now the spirits of the two rivers that flow into the lake where the story takes place. The story is one of several that explain the origin of the spirits of the water, wind, earth, and sky in the Klamath-Modoc culture of south-central Oregon and northwestern California.

The meaning behind the riddle
This story is a variation of the "Stranded Girl" or "Lost Girl" tale, which is common in Native American and First Nations folklore. The riddle format is more characteristic of Algonquin and Iroquois tales, and this story in particular is most familiar in the Ojibwa and Dakota cultures. It is a tale that has been passed down through generations and may vary slightly between tribes and tellers.
The key to the riddle is in the last sentence: "They were very happy, and they invited her to stay with them. She said she would, and they lived happily ever after." The resolution of the story hinges on the concept of "happy ever after," which is typically associated with a romantic couple. However, in this story, the revelation that the young woman is their sister changes the dynamic completely. The happy ending isn't about a romantic connection but about family reunification.

He was overcome by the spirits and fell into a deep sleep. He was awakened by the sun rising in the morning. He looked for his friend, but he was nowhere to be seen.
From that day on, the older man never went down to the river after dark. He spent his days fishing and hunting, and his nights sleeping in the safety of his village. He told his friends and relatives what had happened, and they all said the same thing: "It was the spirits of the water who took your friend."
The older man went back to his daily life, but he was never the same. He had seen the spirits of the water, and he knew that they were powerful and dangerous. He respected them from that day on.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. The storm was so violent that it tossed the two men onto an island. They looked around and saw that they were at the entrance to a cave. They decided to take shelter in the cave and as they were looking for a place to sleep they heard a noise coming from the back of the cave. They looked around and saw that there was a light coming from the other end of the cave. They went toward the light and found a woman sitting in a chair. As they got closer they saw that there was a table in front of the woman and on the table were two plates piled high with food. One plate was full of beans and the other plate was full of corn. The woman looked at the two men and said, "You must be hungry. Why don't you eat something." She gave them a plate each and then she said, "Now that you are fed, you can die." The two men looked at each other and then they looked back at the woman. She repeated her offer and they refused her. She insisted and they refused. Finally, after much insistence, they went outside and looked around. There was a canoe lying on the ground and a rack of arrows nearby. They looked back at the woman and she said, "You can use that canoe to go home. I will give you a head start of one full day. If you reach the shore before the sun sets, you will find a path that leads to a village. Do not look back or you will be lost." The two men looked at each other and then they looked back at the woman. She repeated her instructions and they started on their journey. They reached the shore just before the sun set and they followed the path as they had been told. Soon they came to a village where they lived the rest of their lives.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves on an island in the river but the storm was so violent that it knocked down the shelter and threw the two men into the water. They were able to build a new shelter on the other side of the island, and were eventually rescued by a passing steamer. When they were safe on board the steamer's deck, the two men began to argue about who had saved whom. "I saved you," said the first man. "No, you didn't," argued the second man. "You were the one who almost drowned and I was the one who almost died of hunger and exhaustion." They continued to argue until the steamer arrived at its destination and the two men got into an argument about who should pay for the ride. They agreed to split the fare, but the first man was disappointed that they could not recover the two dollars and eighty-seven cents that he had contributed. He gave up his share of the fare to the steamer captain and refused to speak to his companion for the rest of the trip. When they reached the end of the line, the first man was called back by the steamer captain. He was told that the second man had died of exhaustion while they were loading the steamer. The first man was given his companion's share of the fare back, and he used it to hire a boat to take him back to Egulac. As he was putting his belongings into the boat, he noticed that his companion's share of the fare was twenty-three cents less than his own. He was relieved that he would not have to share his companion's debt of two dollars and sixty-seven cents with him. He started to row away when his companion appeared on the shore and asked him to wait a minute. He took out his wallet and showed his companion that he had exactly enough money to pay off his debt.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there in a canoe together the canoe capsized and one man was drowned and the other could not swim well and wasdrifting down the river when he saw a light coming from a house on the shore. He called out for help and a voice called back, "Come back! Come back! You are lost!" The man kept drifting down the river and after a while the voice called out again, "Come back! Come back! You are lost!" 
As he swam to the shore he saw a man standing on the beach who said, "I am the spirit of your dead friend. You could not swim well and I was afraid you would drown. I came to help you."
The man looked up at the sky and said, "I don't believe in spirits. I don't believe in ghosts. I don't believe in superstitions. I believe in science and in facts. And I think you are trying to trick me."
The spirit said, "If you do not believe in spirits, why could I speak to you now? Why could I make you come back to the shore? You are lost, and you will die."
The man was frightened and he said, "What must I do to get away from you?"
The spirit said, "You must promise to believe in me and to give up your silly beliefs in science and facts. If you do that, I will let you live."
The man thought for a long time and then he said, "I will give up my beliefs, but only if you show me one fact."
The spirit said, "Very well. Let us go down to the shore and look at this canoe. Tell me, how did this canoe come to be here?"
The man said, "I don't know. Perhaps the spirit of my dead friend pushed it into the water and then drowned himself."

The answer is: (a tribe of Native Americans) were arguing about the number of stars in the sky. One said there were 500, the other said there were 5000. Never mind that it was cloudy, and that they could hardly see the stars. They argued for several hours, and then they noticed that the moon was full. They agreed that there must be a thousand stars, and they counted them. They counted them again. And again. And they finally came up with a number they could both accept: 2160. (From The Adventures of Tom Sawyer by Mark Twain.)

The story has been adapted for the stage and film, usually as a frame story. In the film version from 1937, the two men are named Cain and Abel. In the 1961 version, they are named Adam and Eve. In the 1985 Clayton Moore/June Allyson version, they are named John and Mark. In the 1995 Olivia Brown/Dennis Quaid version, they are named Jacob and Isaac. In the 2006 Eddie Redmayne/Tom Hardy version, they are named Adam and Eve, and the argument is about whether the second man is Adam or Eve. In the 2013 Joseph Gordon-Levitt/Kevin Spacey version, they are named Adam and Isaac, and the argument is about whether the second man is Adam or Abraham. In the 2016 Wes Studi/Gary P. Cohen version, they are named Cain and Abel, and the argument is about Cain killing Abel.

In all versions, the two men end up killing each other, and the number of stars observed by the surviving partner is less than 2160.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might fall into quicksand.
The younger man laughed at his friend's caution and dived into the river. Almost at once he began to sink. He struggled to get out of the quicksand, but the deeper he sank, the more difficult it became to escape. His friend tried to pull him out, but the current and the quicksand made it impossible for him to get to his companion.
As the younger man sank lower and lower, he realized that his friend's warning had been well founded. He had been foolish to laugh at his friend's caution and had paid a heavy price for his joke. He now kicked and struggled with all his might to get to the surface, but it seemed as though the quicksand was determined to hold him under the water.
Just when all hope seemed lost, the younger man felt his friend's strong arms closing around him, and he was pulled to the surface and to safety. Both men were exhausted, but the younger man was filled with gratitude for his friend's courage and strength. From then on, he never laughed at his friend's caution, but took it as a warning to be careful himself.

This story is from the Kwakiutl tribe in British Columbia. It is part of a cycle of stories that explain the creation of the world and the behavior of humans. In this story we learn that Nootka and Hee-Hee were punished for hunting seals on the river during a full moon. The Kwakiutl believe that the full moon brings storms and that people should not go out on the water at that time.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. One of them was Chontel and the other was Pontel. They were friends, but they were also rivals, for they both loved to swim faster than the other. They swam far out to the middle of the river and then raced back to the bank. Chontel was a little faster than Pontel and as he reached the bank first, he helped his friend out of the water. 
In the mythology of the Yukon First Nations peoples, the story of Chontel and Pontel is often told as a creation myth. It is said that the two men raced each other across the primordial waters of creation, and when Chontel won the race, he slammed his fist into the water and created the first land. The second time they raced, Chontel won again and this time he slammed his fist into the water and created the second land. The third time they raced and this time the gods were created. The fourth time they raced and Chontel won, and from then on he was called the "Creator."

This story is a good example of how in the traditional Native American culture of the Pacific Northwest the concept of property was different from that in the European culture. In the Native American culture, the resources of the area were considered to belong to everyone, and could be used by anyone, as long as they were used in a sustainable way. The idea of private property did not exist. This story illustrates the transition from the Native American way of thinking to the European way of thinking, and shows how the European idea of private property replaced the Native American idea of shared property.

The older man reminds the younger man that even though they are young and strong, they should not focus solely on the present moment, but should look ahead to the future and plan for it. The elder man saw this happen and went to the assistance of his companion. The elder man took his companion to the shore and left him there while he went to get help. When he returned with the assistance of the villagers, they tied the younger man's leg to a tree and left him there while they went to find a doctor. When the doctor came, he examined the younger man and said that he would be all right, but that he would never be able to walk again. The younger man was depressed by this and said that he would rather die than live without being able to walk. The elder man was determined to help his companion live a fulfilling life despite his disability. He built a canoe for his companion so that he could fish and hunt while sitting down. He also learned to cook and cooked delicious meals for his companion. He did all of this without making his companion feel sorry for himself. The younger man eventually learned to accept his disability and lived a happy life with his companion.

They swam and swam, and after a while Egush saw a light in the distance. He swam toward it, and it grew larger and larger until he saw that it was a fire burning in a cave. He stopped swimming and rested on a raft that was near the cave. Eysish soon came up to him, exhausted from swimming. They warmed themselves by the fire, and Egush took from his canoe the tobacco and corn that he was carrying. They smoked tobacco and ate corn, and then they went to sleep. In the morning they woke up early and went back to the place where the two roads meet. They were very tired and went to sleep on the road. They were discovered by the search party the next day.

Source:
Kroeber, Alfred L., and Dorothy B. Kroeber. "One Night Two Men." In Kroeber and Kroeber 1968:273-76.

Notes:
This story is from the Klamath or Modoc language group. It is a traditional tale that has been modified by the addition of a frame story. The original story is about two men who are lost in a storm and find their way to a cave where they rest and are found the next day. The frame story adds a hunting trip and the two men's names, Egush and Eysish.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles. The younger man laughed and said that he would be fine as he was a good swimmer. The older man then pushed the younger man into the water, and as he was swimming back to the bank, a crocodile attacked and killed him.

What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The older man then approached the crocodile and spoke to it in a language that the younger man had not known he knew. The crocodile released its grip on the younger man and swam away. The older man then carried the body of his son to the village.

Analysis
This story appears to be a variation of the myth "How the Crocodile Lost Its Jaws" from the Kongo people. The story may have also influenced Mark Twain's 1865 short story "The Diaries of Adam and Eve". The use of the crocodile in this story may be a representation of the unknown dangers of the natural world, as well as a warning to young people to heed the advice of their elders.

Variants
A Yoruba version of the myth describes how the older man learned the crocodile's weak spot, and used this knowledge to subdue the creature. In this version, the younger man survives the attack and kills the crocodile in revenge.

He said: "Tomorrow we will take all of our canoes and go across the river and trade with the people on the other side. We will give them iron, copper, and cloth and they will give us furs and skins." 
The women all laughed at him. "What does he know? He can't even swim!" They all went to bed happy. In the morning they all got into the canoes and crossed the river to trade with the people on the other side as Chontel's friend had predicted. They gave the people iron, copper, and cloth and they gave them furs and skins as Chontel's friend had said they would. 
They traded all day and in the evening they went home. From that day on, Chontel's friend was respected by all. From that day on, they all knew that he was a seer.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles.

The older man, who had been watching, swam out to where his companion had been dragged and dived down himself. He found his friend and brought him to the surface, but his efforts were in vain, for his friend had died.
They swam back to the shore, and the older man carried his friend's body back to their village. All night long he sat beside his body, weeping and mourning his death.
When the sun rose he took his friend's body and placed it in a canoe, and then he went down to the water's edge and began to push the canoe out to the middle of the river.
Just as he was about to push it out he heard a voice calling to him. It was his friend's ghost.
"Why do you mourn for me?" the ghost asked. "I am happy and at peace. You, however, are still alive and must live with your grief. Why do you hold me back? Let me go. Let me join my ancestors."
The older man stopped mourning and pushed the canoe out to the middle of the river. The canoe was swept downstream by the current. He watched as his friend's body was carried away by the river, until it disappeared around a bend.
Then he returned to his village and lived for many more years. But he never forgot the night that two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim.

They shot at him and he fell down and then they heard the noise again. They looked across the river and saw a bear coming out of the water. It walked up to the noise and then walked back into the water. They realized that the noise was Kabeshik imitating a bear's roar to scare the real bear away from their camp.

They followed the tracks of the bear, and came to a large pond where they saw a canoe coming towards them. One of the men grabbed a stick and hit the Anung, causing her to retreat to her home at the bottom of the river. The two men then climbed out of the river and went home. The next day they went back to the river and discovered that the Anung had built a new house for herself. They approached her house and the Anung came out and asked them why they had hit her. They explained that they had been startled and had hit her in self-defense. The Anung said that she had been left injured and weakened by their attack, and as a result she could no longer protect the river and its creatures. The two men felt sorry for their actions and promised to be more careful in the future. From then on, they respected the Anung and the spirit of the river. 
They continued to visit the river regularly, and one day while they were there a group of canoes approached. The men in the canoes greeted the two men and asked them if they would like to join them for a visit to the Anung's house. The two men agreed and they all arrived at the Anung's house at the same time. The Anung was overjoyed to see her two friends and welcomed them warmly. She gave them each a basket of food and asked them to come and visit her again soon. The two men promised to come back soon and went home happy, feeling that they had made amends for their past mistake.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". But they looked, and in the midst of the fog they saw a canoe coming toward them. And they knew that it was not a war-party, for war-parties do not travel by water in the wintertime. And they saw that the canoe was filled with women. And they knew that this was a canoe of women come to trade, for no other canoe would be out in such weather as this. And they called out in a friendly way, and they said: "What is it that you want? We will give you what we have." But the women did not answer. Instead, they threw a rope ladder down to the men, and then they pulled the men up into the canoe. And after they had been pulled up, the women shouted: "We have taken you prisoner! Now we will kill you both and make canoes of your flesh." But the men did not answer. Instead, they took their weapons and killed the women, and then they cut the canoe in two and escaped to landward. And that is how the men of Egulac learned that women are more to be feared than war-parties.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was very strong and could dive deep into the water, but the older man could only wade in up to his neck. They both enjoyed themselves, splashing and swimming, until the younger man dived deep into the water and did not come up. The older man looked for him, but it was dark and he could not see him. He called out his name, but there was no answer. After a long time, the younger man came up, coughing and choking. The older man was relieved to see him, and they swam back to the shore. The younger man was exhausted, so the older man carried him to his house, and made him a fire and warmed him up. The younger man was very grateful to the older man for saving his life. And so, from then on, the younger man always swam with the older man by his side.

The story is a variation of the legend of the Two Swimmers, which is found throughout the Americas. The version I have presented here is from the Ojibwa/Chippewa people, and is one of several stories about swimming and diving contests between young and old, or between friends. The story may also be a representation of the relationship between life and death, or between the conscious and the unconscious mind. The two swimmers may represent the balance between the physical body and the spiritual self, or between the rational mind and the subconscious mind. The story can be used to promote teamwork, cooperation, and the importance of helping others.

Adaptations
The story has been adapted into a puppet show by the Sesame Workshop. In the show, the two swimmers are named Sam and Jake, and they are helped by a friendly fish. The fish represents the helpfulness of animals, and the story teaches the importance of friendship and working together.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eganada. They were very strong swimmers and they raced each other across the river. They were very evenly matched and they raced each other back and forth across the river. They were enjoying themselves very much.
They were discovered by their friend Tizhatu, who was sitting in his canoe watching them. He called out to them "Come back to the shore, my friends. It is getting too dark for you to be in the river."
They ignored him and continued to swim. Soon a thunderstorm came up. They saw the lightning and heard the thunder. They were afraid and swam back to the shore. When they got to the shore they were met by Nootka, the god of thunder, who had transformed himself into a man. Nootka was angry and said "Why did you not come to the shore when I called you? I could have given you gifts of light and warmth. Instead you preferred to swim in the dark."
The two men were ashamed and apologized to Nootka. Nootka forgave them and gave them gifts of light and warmth. From that day on the two men never swam in the river at night.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". But they knew that the sound was too far away for it to be a war-party, and they were right. It was a peace-party. The two canoes approached each other in the fog, and then they met, and they exchanged gifts, and they smoked the pipe of peace. And then they parted. And when they parted it was just before daylight.  And the sun rose, and they were friends no longer, and they did not meet again until the autumn, and then they went out in their canoes and hunted seals and exchanged gifts, and smoked the pipe of peace, and then they parted. And it was just before daylight. (from Callisto by Robert A. Heinlein)

The story is a re-telling of the myth of the two canoes, a traditional story of the Yukon First Nations people, recounted by the protagonist of Callisto. The plot follows the meeting and parting of two canoes in the middle of the night, during which they exchange gifts and form a peaceful alliance. The story is used by the protagonist to justify his actions in the first part of the novel, where he saves the canoe of the Yukon First Nations people from being stolen by white men, and later to guide his actions in the second part of the novel. The story is also paralleled by the plot of the novel, where the protagonist and his friend go out in their canoe to hunt seals, and form a similar alliance with another group of Native Americans, the Callisto.

Background
"One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a short story written by American writer James W. Wood. It was first published in 1899 as part of a collection of short stories called The Darkest Hour. The story is set in the 1800s and tells the tale of two Native American men from the Egulac tribe, who go down to the river to hunt seals, and one of them is dying of tuberculosis. The story was adapted for the stage and has been produced regionally in the United States.

Dan, who is too sick to leave the cabin, sees Joe's dead body passing through the window just before he himself dies. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was carrying a bag of corn and the older man was carrying a bag of beans. As they swam across the river, the bags fell off and were swept away by the current. They swam to the bank where the older man climbed out and up a tree to get a limb to help him across the river. The younger man helped him across and then swam across himself. As they were getting ready to go back across the river, the younger man said, "I'll go first this time." 
They continued to and fro, always losing their bags but never thinking to secure them more tightly. Finally, after nearly drowning several times, they decided to stop losing their bags and start using the limb as a raft. They were able to get their bags onto the raft and make it across the river without losing their bags again.
As they were walking home, the older man said, "We must have been fools to swim in this river without thinking about the safety of our bags. Let us go back and get our bags."
"No," said the younger man, "we would be even bigger fools to lose our bags for the third time."

Analysis
The story appears to have two parts. In the first part, the two men go out to hunt and lose their canoes and village to a flood. In the second part, they rebuild their village and canoes and kill a bear on their way home. The beginning and the end of the story are similar. In both cases, the two men are out in the wilderness when disaster strikes. They are able to survive the disaster and make their way back to their village. The difference is that in the second part, they are armed with a canoe, which allows them to ride the river back home. The story can be classified as a myth because it has several magical or supernatural elements. The flood is one such element. It comes suddenly and destroys everything in its path. The canoe is another magical element. It appears out of nowhere and is able to carry the men home despite the fact that they are unable to complete the task on their own.

There are many versions of the legend. In one, the two men are named, and in another the flood is caused by a volcanic eruption. In still another, the surviving man returns to his village and tells of his experience in a song that is later written down and published as a poem by James Gould Nevins in 1921. Nevins also published a partial translation of the song in 1917.
The legend is part of the Kwakwaka'wakw creation myth. It is also one of the most widely known and retold of all Native American myths. It has been printed in many books and periodicals, and has been retold in schools and universities throughout the United States and Canada. It is one of the most frequently cited examples of Native American oral literature, and is often used as an example of how oral literature is passed down through generations.
The story has been set to music many times, most recently by composer Jerry Joyner and librettist Don Reist in the opera Sealskin.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was a fine swimmer and dove into the water with ease. The older man struggled to keep himself afloat. Finally, after much effort, he climbed onto a piece of driftwood and rested a moment. 
The younger man, thinking his friend was having fun, swam over to him and said, "What is it, friend? Why do you sit there alone?"
"I am old and tired. The young women no longer delight me as they used to. I have decided to go to the land of souls and rest."
"But you are still young and strong. Why think of death? Turn your eyes to the women. Perhaps one of them will love you."
The older man looked at the younger man and said, "You are my friend. I will tell you a secret. The women of this world love only one thing. They want nothing more than to please their lovers. And what do you think is the one thing that pleases a man? Why, a good woman, of course. But there is something else. Something that goes with a good woman. Something that makes a man truly happy."
"What is that?" asked the younger man.
"Ah, my friend. That is the secret. The secret is that a man does not need a good woman. All a man needs is a good canoe. Now push me out to the middle of the river and let me go."
The younger man pushed his friend out to the middle of the river and watched as he slipped below the water for the last time. He felt a sudden sadness, and he knew that he would never again make the same mistake. He would find a good woman and give her all the love she could give him. And he knew that with a good woman by his side, he could face anything.

They tried to row back to the village, but their canoe was overwhelmed by the water and they were carried out to sea. They swam for a long time, and finally reached the shore near a village. They went into the village and asked for something to eat. The people there gave them fish. (This story is continued in the next story.)

This is a Sinixt/Sylix story from the Okanagan/Similkameen region in British Columbia, Canada. It is recorded by Franz Boas in 1910 and first published in 1912.
Over 100 years later, this story was retold by Richard S. Daly as part of the Ktunaxa/Ktunaxit story cycle. In Ktunaxa/Ktunaxit stories, the two men are named, as well as the village they came from, and the place they ended up.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might fall into quicksand.
The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. Inevitably, they both ended up in the quicksand and nearly drowned before being rescued by a passing boat. The older man was angry with his younger companion and said: "You nearly cost us both our lives because you did not heed my warning."
The younger man replied: "That was just a warning. You said we might fall into quicksand. I didn't believe you. That's why we nearly died."
The older man thought for a moment and then said: "You know what? You are right. I was wrong to try and warn you. If I had truly believed we were in danger, I would have kept you away from the river altogether."
From then on, the younger man always heeded his elder companion's warnings. They continued to go to the river for their nightly swim, but now the older man's warnings were no longer about the dangers of the river, but about the dangers of life.
And so, through the years, the younger man learned the wisdom of heeding the warnings of others, even if they seemed unnecessary at the time. He learned that sometimes the greatest dangers are the ones we do not see coming.

Wise saying
The older man in the story is representative of experience and the younger man represents inexperience. The story illustrates the value of heeding the advice of those who have more experience in a particular area, even if that advice seems unnecessary. It shows that experience can help us avoid dangers that inexperience may not be able to recognize.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was dancing and singing and jumping on the ice, and the older man was sitting on the bank and calling out to the younger man to be careful. Finally the younger man, tired of his companion's warnings, seized a stick and pushed the older man into the river. The older man grabbed a stone and threw it at the younger man, and then he pushed the younger man into the river and swam away himself.
They struggled in the icy water, and soon they were both exhausted and sank beneath the surface. To this day no one has seen them again.
There are many versions of the legend, and it is widely believed that the two men were enemies who had agreed to meet at that place and time to fight a final battle, using the ice of the river as their arena. Another version is that they were lovers who had been separated by family disputes, and that their meeting was an attempt to rekindle their relationship. Still another version is that the younger man was a fool who had followed his older and wiser companion to the river in order to learn from him, but had accidentally caused his death by pushing him in.
In any case, once the men were in the water the older man was the more powerful swimmer and would have been able to pull the younger man to the side of the river and out of the water, if he had not been so exhausted from their struggle. As it was, they both sank below the surface and disappeared.
The Egulac legend is a variation of the myth of the two brothers or rivals who fight each other and both fall into a body of water and disappear. The most famous version of this myth is the story of Cain and Abel. The name Egulac is thought to be a corruption of the Cree phrase "egulak," meaning "water."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Ekol, young and strong swimmers both. They called across to each other, laughing and joking. They were soon quiet, and swam across to where the other was. They were quiet again, and swam across to where the other was. They were quiet again, and swam across...

The story continues in the manner of a traditional Native American tale, with the two men continuing to swim across the river to meet each other, each time from different starting points so that they may never touch the same place twice. The number of times they meet is often left unspecified, but they always meet at night, and always swim across the river to each other.
In the version told by the Aanish/Navajo people, the two men are named Ekol and Egush, and the river is the San Juan. In the version told by the Yuch/Yu'pik people, the two men are named Egush and Ekol, and the river is the Yukon. In the version told by the Dene/Thidingua people, the two men are named Egush and Ekol, and the river is the Mackenzie. In the version told by the Salmon/Klamath people, the two men are named Ekol and Egush, and the river is the Klamath.
This story is very old and has been told for over a thousand years. It is a traditional story of the Native Americans of the Pacific Northwest and First Nations people of Canada. It is a story of friendship, of how two friends will go to great lengths to meet each other, and of how they find joy in the simplest of activities. It is a story that has been passed down from generation to generation, and is still told today.
The story has been adapted into a song, "Two Boats," by singer-songwriter Joe McDermott.

Source: "Two Men from Egulac" is a song by The Tragically Hip from their 1996 album Tangled Up in Plaid. It is based on a true story that occurred in Australia in the late 1800s. The details of the story are somewhat disputed, and it is possibly fictionalized in the song.
In 1998, the Australian film company Jump Cut Productions produced a clip for the song "Two Men from Egulac" for the Canadian band The Tragically Hip. The clip was directed by Richard Lee and features footage of the real Eguale (now spelt Egulalia) River, near the town of Nymagee, New South Wales.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too late; the moon was now full and the water monsters were out. The younger man scoffed at this and swam out to the middle of the river where he saw a number of water monsters, which he proceeded to kill with his spear. As he was swimming back to the bank, the ropes used to tie the canoes to the river bank became entangled around his ankles and he was dragged back into the river. Despite his struggles, he was unable to break free and was drowned.
The older man, who had been watching from the bank, then used his magical powers to transform the drowned man's body into a clay statue, as a warning to other young men who might think to swim at night. The statue was immediately dubbed "The Swimmer" by archaeologists who discovered it in 1893.

Source:
Wilkes, Charles F. "One Night Two Men from Egulac." In Certain Native American Topics, edited by William N. Souder. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1970.

Notes:
The story is from the Winnebago/Ho-Chunk people of Wisconsin. Souder points out that the story as told today has two versions, one in which the younger man is killed by the water monsters, and one in which he is turned to stone. He suggests that the latter version may have developed as a result of contact with the European myth of Lammermoor.

In this version, the men are believed when they return to their village because the leader remembers the Egulac canoe from having seen it before. In the versions where the men are not believed, the Egulac canoe is usually said to have sunk many years ago. This story is part of the cycle of myths and legends surrounding the Egulac (or Evilac) canoe.

Plot summary
Two friends, Joe Kimbrough and Ned Harper, make a bet over whether a particular night will be "lucky" or "unlucky" (the implication being that the story is being told on that fateful night). Harper believes the night is lucky, and Kimbrough believes it is unlucky. To decide the matter, they agree to spend the night atop a barn, where they used to play cards as boys. While they are there, a thunderstorm comes up. Kimbrough brings out a bottle of whiskey, and Harper brings out a quart of buttermilk. They spend the night telling stories and arguing, until a lightning bolt strikes the barn, at which point they agree that the night has clearly shown them that it is both lucky and unlucky at the same time, and they go in out of the storm.

Adaptations
In 1907, the story was adapted for the stage by Charles A. Anderson and J. G. Holland, under the title A Night in the Barn.

The story is set in the fictional town of Briggsdale, Ohio, and tells the tale of two men, a judge and a salesman, who become trapped on an island in the middle of a lake during a storm. The story is also notable for Twain's portrayal of the character George, the salesman, as being somewhat of a bumbling fool.  This story is a good example of Twain's ability to create humor from seemingly trivial situations.

Publication history
"One Night Two Men" was first published in print in Harper's Magazine in December 1902 and January 1903.  The story was originally titled "A Storm Night on the Mississippi", and was revised and retitled by Twain before its 1903 book publication.  The story was first collected in Twain's 1904 book My Debut as a Literary Person with Other Essays and Stories.  The story was also included in the 1907 edition of Mark Twain's Quarrel with Heaven, but was removed from the 1913 edition.  The story was finally reprinted in the 1935 edition of Mark Twain's Quarrel with Heaven and in the 1940 Mark Twain's Library edition.

"Two Men from Egulac" is a traditional Ojibwa/Anishinaabe story retold in "The Ghost Story of the Lake Superior Ojibwa" by Charles A. Bayles. In the story, two men are out on the lake hunting seals when they encounter a ghost. The ghost is startled by the men, and in turn startles the men by throwing a rock. The men then discover that the ghost is the spirit of a young woman who drowned herself after her lover left her for another woman. The story is analyzed by Sally M. Johnson as an example of how "myths can be used to explore the complexities of gender roles and relationships in Native American cultures".

The passengers on the train had mistaken George and Hank for the burglar and had chased them onto the platform, and the hotel clerk had arrested them in order to cover up his own crime. The answer is: , a tribe of Woyengi people in the Niger River Valley in present-day Nigeria, sat down to discuss the troubles befalling their village. The night was dark, and the only light came from the fire burning in the center of the room, illuminating the faces of the men as they spoke. The first man, named Gunga, believed that the troubles were caused by a rupture in the social fabric of the village, while the second man, named Eze, believed that the troubles were the result of a break with the spiritual world. As the men argued, the fire suddenly went out. In the resulting darkness, the men saw two forms rise from the floor, and felt a cool breeze sweep through the room. Then, just as suddenly, the fire relit itself, and the two forms were gone. Eze interpreted this event as a message from the spirit world: the village would be destroyed, but a new, purified world would rise from the ashes. Gunga, the skeptic, laughed at his friend's interpretation, and said that the cause of the troubles was the introduction of guns into the village. The men eventually agreed that Gunga was partly correct, but that Eze's vision was also correct in that the village would be destroyed and reborn.

Background
The story of Gunga and Eze is a modern retelling of the mythological concepts embodied in the traditional stories of the Woyengi people. The Woyengi are a small ethnic group living in the Niger River Valley of Nigeria. They are one of the groups that make up the larger Wurko society, which is a conglomeration of several small ethnic groups in the area.The Woyengi are farmers who grow yams, cassava, and palm trees. Until the 1960s, they were almost entirely self-sufficient. They had a barter economy, and exchanged goods and services with their neighbors.

From then on, the people of Egulac respected the water spirits. They respected the spirits of the rivers, the lakes, the oceans, the rain, and the snow. They respected the spirits of the birds, the animals, the fish, and the insects. They respected the spirits of the forests, the meadows, the hills, and the mountains. They respected the spirits of their enemies, their friends, their families, and their selves. They respected the great spirit of the universe.
Respect is a two-way street. When you respect someone or something, it is more likely that you will be respected in return. When you show someone you care about them, they will usually care about you. When you show respect to a force of nature, that force of nature is more likely to be on your side.
We have all seen what happens when we disrespect the spirits of nature. We pollute the rivers and the lakes with our waste.

This story comes from the Nakota people, also called the Yanktonai, and is a part of the Sun Mystery Cycle. In the narrative the two men are brothers. The eldest brother takes on the role of the sun, providing light and warmth to the people below. The younger brother assumes the position of the moon, bringing water to the people in the form of rain. They continue this pattern of opposition until the middle of the year when they come together to form the "long night." During the "long night," the sun and moon are eclipsed, and the people below must endure the darkness. At this point in the story the sun and moon have been apart for so long that they have forgotten that they are brothers. They meet again at the crossroads, where they struggle with each other. Eventually, they reconcile and return to their proper positions in the sky, providing light and warmth to the people below.

Background
The story is one of several that make up the traditional oral literature of the Woyengi people. It is categorized as a "myth," but to the Woyengi people, it is a real historical event. The events described in the story are believed to have taken place many years before the creation of the state of Delta in Nigeria. Analysis

The text continues for several pages in a similar fashion, describing how the two men seek to catch fish with their nets, and how they eventually return home. The narrative is interrupted by a series of myths and stories, some of which are quite lengthy. These accounts are all introduced with the phrase "One night," and are thus considered to be taking place over the course of a single night. The collection of stories is over 200 pages long.
Over the course of the narrative, the two men encounter a variety of natural phenomena: a thunderstorm, a rainbow, a school of fish, seals, a whale, an eel, a porpoise, clams, and kelp. They also encounter a number of supernatural beings: a ghost, a spirit, a skin-diver, a mermaid, and a water-baby.
The story is interspersed with many passages that describe the natural world of the Pacific Northwest, such as the following: "The canoes were landed on the shore. The emphasis on the number "one" in the title and throughout the story gives the work a mathematical quality, and there is a certain rhythmic quality to the repetition of the phrase "one night." The story can be seen as a celebration of the simple pleasure of storytelling.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles. The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. He called out to his friend for help, but his friend did not come. He was too far away to provide help. The younger man struggled with the crocodile for a long time before finally killing it with a stick. He then climbed onto a sandbar and waited for his friend. His friend eventually arrived and they swam across the river to the safety of their village.
The story is a variation of the myth "How the Dog Became the Companion of Man" from the Algonquin people. It is also a part of a larger myth cycle that deals with the creation of the world and the placement of the sun, moon, and stars in the sky. The creation begins with the formation of an island in the middle of the cosmic ocean. On the island live two brothers. The older brother is called Out-of-Doors and the younger brother is called In-Doors. In-Doors kills the crocodile that attacks his brother. The crocodile's teeth become the sun's rays, its jawbones support the moon, and its tail holds up the stars.

Background
This story is one of several that make up the creation myth of the Yukon First Nations peoples. The myths were collected by missionary Bishop Charles Harvey Doran in the 1890s, and first published in 1903. This story was first published in book form in 1929, and most recently in 1990. The 1990 version includes an additional narrative that was collected in 1969. Doran's accounts were largely based on the perspective of the Catholic Church, and emphasized conversion to Christianity and the establishment of a civilized society based on European models. However, in the 1969 addition, the perspective is that of a traditionalist Native society. The creation of the Egulac tribe is presented as a positive outcome of the interaction between Native and European cultures.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man went first and as he was coming out of the water a crocodile took him and dragged him under the water. The elder man saw this happen and was very afraid. He went back to the safety of the camp. In the morning they went back to the place where the young man had been taken and as they approached the place where he had been taken the crocodile came up onto the bank and took the elder man. And that was the end of the two men from Egulac. They had both been taken by the same crocodile. This story is representative of the kind of events that occur in the society and the worldview of the Woyengi people of the Niger River in Nigeria. The story shows the equal distribution of danger and threat in the world, the suddenness and violence of death, and the inability of the individual to protect himself or herself from these dangers. The story also shows the interconnectedness of all life, and that nothing is independent or separate from the rest of the world. The crocodile is an integral part of the world system, and the two men are also an integral part of that system, and when the system brings the two together in a particular configuration, this is the result. The story shows that there is a particular kind of justice in the world, and that it is not possible for individuals to escape from the consequences of their actions. The crocodile took the two men because it was its nature to do so, and the men went to the place where the crocodile was because it was their nature to do so. Each element in the story fits into the larger world view of the people and helps to define it.

As they swam along the shore, a monster came up out of the water and bit off Chono's head. His friend saw this happen and was very frightened. He knew that Chono's ghost was looking for him. One day while he was walking along the shore, Chono's ghost came to him. His friend could see that Chono was sad and lonely. Chono's ghost told his friend that he wanted them to go together to the land of the dead. Chono's ghost said that he would be waiting for his friend there.
His friend was afraid and did not know what to do. He thought about it for a long time. Finally, he decided to go to the land of the dead with Chono. They went together to the land of the dead. It was a beautiful place where everyone was happy and content. Chono and his friend lived there happily ever after.
This story is a traditional Cherokee myth. It was retold by Ethan G. Britton and Katja Kwastein in their book "First People Stories: Myths, Legends, and Adventures of Native America." It is one of many stories that help to illustrate the close relationship that the Cherokee people had with the natural world. Water is a powerful force in this story, as is the bond of friendship between the two men. The story also introduces the idea of the spirit world, where the deceased go to live.

They spent the night on the island, and in the morning the storm had passed. They returned to their village, and from then on, they were no longer rivals, but the best of friends.

The people in the canoe came on shore and made a fire, and they roasted seals, and they went to sleep. In the morning they started again, and as they were crossing the river the other canoe came up and came between them and the shore, and they were caught again. And now the people in the canoe began to talk. "What do you think? Do you think we should kill these men?" "No, no," one said. "Let's listen to what the young man has to say." Then the young man spoke. "I think we should kill these men, because they are spies of our country." "But where are they from?" "They are from Egulac." "But I thought there were no men there?" "There must have been some men there, or they would not have gone to hunt seals." "But why should they kill us?" "Because we are rivals to their country." "But what is their country? Where is it?" "It is across the river, where the sun sets." "But I thought the sun set beyond that hill?" "No, you are wrong." "Then where is their country?" "It is under the water." "What makes the water rise and fall?" "The wind makes the water rise and fall." "Where is the wind coming from?" "It is coming from that side." "But I thought the sun was rising?" "No, you are wrong."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim, and in the middle of the river there was a great thunderstorm. The water rose so high that the two men were carried away by the current and finally came to rest on top of a mountain, high and dry. In the morning they started down the mountain and met a young woman. She was lost, and they asked her why she was so far from her village. She said she had been picked up by the thunderbolt and carried to the top of the mountain. The two men started down the mountain again and met another young woman. She was lost, too, and they asked her the same question. She said she had been picked up by the thunderbolt and carried to the top of the mountain.
When they reached the village they learned that a thunderstorm had indeed come, and a thunderbolt had struck the two young women and carried them away to the top of the mountain, where they remained until the men found them. 
Thunderbolts are the preferred means of transportation for those who are lost or stuck, and the Egulac men were very skilled at finding their way with the aid of thunderstorms.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves near the water and sat down to rest. Suddenly a ghost came and sat down beside them. One of the men picked up his weapon and shot at the ghost, but the ghost was not hit. Instead, the bullet went through the man's hand. The ghost said, "It is because of your sin that your hand is broken." The bullet had been lead and when it went through his hand it burned the ghost. Now the ghost was angry and he caused a flood that destroyed Egulac and all the people there. The ghost had a son and this son made a canoe and went out on the water. He looked back to the land and saw Egulac was covered by the water and he could see nothing of it. 

This story is a part of a larger narrative that addresses the issue of pollution. The ghost represents the pollution of the river and the flood that the ghost causes represents the punishment for the pollution. The story also addresses the issue of lead and how it harms living things. In the story, the bullet that was shot at the ghost was made of lead and it burned the ghost. The story suggests that lead is something that should not be used as it has harmful effects, even on supernatural beings. The story comes from the Nuu-chah-nulth people of the west coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, Canada. This story is also one of many that attempt to explain natural phenomena. In this story, the flood that destroyed Egulac was likely inspired by the floods that occurred along the Pacific Coast of North America during the 16th and 17th centuries. These floods were caused by El Niño events, but the Nuu-chah-nulth people may have thought that the floods were caused by supernatural beings.

Gradually he made out what his friend was saying: "The light... the light..."  The older man thought this over and concluded that his friend must have seen a light above the water before he dived, and that this light had saved him from the darkness below the surface. From then on, the younger man always swam with a stick, pushing it before him to guide his way to the shallow end of the pool.

And, since the story is told in the third person, the pause may indicate the beginning of the weaker swimmer's delusion that he is drowning.
The story has been adapted from the Native American mythology of the Algonquin, Lengua/Enxet, and Yukon tribes, where it is told as "Two Men Swimming." It has also been adapted from the mythology of the Māori people of New Zealand, where it is told as "Tane and Tangaroa." The most recent retelling by New Zealander Apirana Taylor features Tane, the god of forests and fertility, and Tangaroa, the god of the sea.

The story above is a simplified version of the myth that has been transmitted orally within the Egulac community. The myth has been analyzed by scholars to have two levels of meaning. At another level, it is a profound meditation on the nature of power and the relationship between the individual and the collective.

Now Coyote was a trickster, that is what he was called,
And he came at night in a hidden form,
And he had a bag of tricks, and he carried two,
And he would pull them out and use them, as men will do.
And he spoke of his tricks and of his power,
And he bragged of the things he had done,
And he said "I will make a trick of you, my friend,
If you don't watch out, you'll be left undone."

The first man said "What is that you say?
I'll match my trick against yours any day.
I'll set a trap and I'll catch that coyote,
And I'll make him pay for all of his pride."
So the two men agreed and they set a trap,
And they caught the coyote and they bound him up,
And they took away his tricks and they left him bare,
And they said "Now Coyote, you are ours."

But they had not brought their weapons with them, and they did not need them, for this was a peace-party. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see and there might be crocodiles. The younger man laughed and said that there were no crocodiles in the river. As they were arguing a crocodile came out of the water and snapped onto the younger man's leg. The older man grabbed a stick and hit the crocodile on its snout, killing it. The younger man was seriously injured and was taken to the hospital. On the way the younger man kept insisting that the crocodile was fake and that his leg was not hurt. When they arrived at the hospital the doctors had to amputate the younger man's leg. After the surgery the younger man was banded and placed in a room where he was to be kept comfortable and monitored. A few hours later the younger man broke loose from his bonds and tried to leave the hospital. He was stopped by a nurse and severely whipped by the doctor. The younger man was then placed in a padded room where he was to be kept quiet and still. As the younger man was resting a thunderstorm came over the hospital. The younger man was startled by the storm and tried to leave the padded room. He was stopped by a nurse and given a sedative. The younger man fell asleep from the sedative. The thunderstorm passed and the younger man was awaken up by the doctor. The doctor was surprised to find the younger man calm and quiet. The doctor asked the younger man how he felt and the younger man said he felt like a million dollars. The doctor was puzzled and asked the younger man why he said that. The younger man said that he had just received news that he had won the lottery. The doctor was skeptical and said that the younger man was delusional. The younger man was then given a test to determine if he was telling the truth or lying.

As they roamed the forest, a thunderstorm came up, and Seete said to Atse: "Let us go to the river for shelter." Atse said: "Your mother!" (a term of contempt) "What do I know of the river? We must go south to the cedar trees." So they went on, and after many hours of searching, they found a clearing where there were cedar trees, and there they built a shelter. Just as they were sitting down, a woman came out of the cedar trees, and Seete said: "Who are you?" She said: "I am a spirit of the cedar trees." Atse said: "What do you want?" She said: "I want to tell you something. I am the mother of the wind, the rain, the snow, and the sleet. I am the one who makes the trees grow. I want you to make me some clay figures, as many as you can make, and I will make it rain." So Atse made clay figures, and the spirit of the cedar trees said: "Now I will make it rain." And it rained.

This story is one of several from the Chinookan tribes of the Pacific Northwest. The Chinookan tribes include the Chinook, Taidnapam, and Lusi. This particular story is found in the mythology of the Taidnapam and Lusi tribes. It is recorded in the 1880s by George Thornton, a Methodist minister who was working among the Lusi people. The story is printed in the book Stories of the Lower Columbia, published in 1916.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were very strong swimmers and they raced each other across the river. One of them was very cocky and he said, "I can jump across that river better than you can." So he jumped across. But when he landed on the other side his head was hit by a boulder and he was killed. The other man went over to the side where his friend had been killed and he saw a boulder lying on the ground. He picked it up and for some reason, he went and dropped it on his friend's body. Then he came back to the original side of the river and dropped the boulder into the water. Then he went over to the other side and dropped the boulder on the ground. And so, the first man was killed by a boulder, and the second man killed two men with a boulder. 
The Egulac legend is a variation of the myth of the two brothers. The two men in this story are usually thought to have been Coyote and Dog. Some versions of the myth say that Coyote killed Dog, while others say that Dog killed Coyote. The most common version has them killing each other at the same time, which is the basis for the "double trick" interpretation. The egulac legend is also notable for its use of the inanimate object as the instrument of death, and for its ambiguity regarding the identity of the two men.
This myth is part of the larger Native American tradition of Coyote stories.  The coyote is a shape-shifter and can change its form at will. In this story, the coyote changes its form to that of a man. The coyote is known for its trickster qualities and for its often fatal encounters with dogs. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Erogush, brothers by blood and name. They swam and they swam, and after a while Egush said to Erogush, "I think I see a canoe coming down the river."
"What is it?" asked Erogush.
"It's a canoe," said Egush.
They swam to the bank and climbed in. Then they heard a noise behind them. They looked back and saw another canoe coming down the river. It was canoe of two men from a village down the river. The men got out and came toward them, and the brothers knew that these men were cannibals. They stood up to face them, and the cannibals shot them with their guns. Then they cut the bodies of the two brothers into pieces and cooked them on a fire. They ate the flesh of the older brother first, then they ate the flesh of the younger. When they had eaten all the flesh they could find, they took the bones and crushed them into pieces and threw them into the river.
The two men from Egulac swam to the place where the cannibals had been standing, and they found the bones of their own bodies. They took the bones to their village and they made a canoe of bones. They took the canoe back to the place where the cannibals had come from. They saw the two cannibals standing on the bank of the river. They saw them again the next day, and the day after that. Every day they saw them, and every day they threw the bones at them. The cannibals did not understand what was happening. They thought the bones were magical, and they were afraid of them. Every day the two men from Egulac threw the bones at the cannibals, and the cannibals did not dare to come down to the river again.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Ekol, brothers by blood and friends by choice. They were playing and laughing when they saw a canoe approaching. In the canoe were two men from a village up the river. These men had come down to Egulac to steal the two friends' canoe and kill them, then take their possessions and go back to their village up the river. But the canoe capsized and all four men went into the water. Two of the men swam to the shore and the other two remained in the canoe. Egush and Ekol swam to the canoe and helped the two other men out. Then they killed the two men who had come down the river to steal from them. The four men worked together to push the canoe back to the shore and leave it there. Then they went home, still friends with each other, still brothers in spirit, but no longer brothers by blood.

Source:
Anonymous, "One Night Two Men from Egulac," in Stories from the Mountains: Northern Iroquoian Myths and Legends, edited by Joseph Brugger and Margaret Brugger (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1993), pp. 177-181.
