One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man went first and as he was coming out of the water a crocodile seized him and dragged him back into the river. The elder man saw this happen and went home to get his weapons. When he returned he shot the crocodile, killing it, but the crocodile had left his prey behind and the younger man was gone. The elder man then took his canoe and went out onto the river and saw a hippopotamus coming toward him. He shot at the hippopotamus, but it was a female with a young one by her side. The female hippopotamus charged the canoe, forcing the man back onto the shore, where he died.

The story, as it has been transmitted today, is that of a conflict between two men and the animals they encounter. The setting is the river Egulac, which is a variant spelling of the word "Egbara," which means "water." The two men go down to the river for a swim. The younger man goes first and is killed by a crocodile. The elder man sees this happen and goes home to get his weapons. When he returns he finds the crocodile has gone and the younger man is gone, too. The crocodile has taken the younger man's body away to feed to its young, as is their custom. The elder man then sees a hippopotamus and her baby coming toward him. He shoots the hippopotamus, killing the calf. The mother then charges the canoe, forcing the man back onto the shore, where he dies.

One night two men from Egulac went out hunting; they were Atqua and Sahqua, and they had taken with them only one light. They had gone a long distance, and as they were crossing a wide, open, moonlit plain, suddenly they heard a strange sound. It was a sort of humming or buzzing, like the sound of bees. They listened, and it seemed to come from the ground below them. They were very far from home now, and the only other person they knew to be in the country was a squaw named Wohaw. They decided to look for her, and they went towards the place where they thought her village might be. As they approached it, they heard the same sound, and suddenly a bright light shot up in the air, and a voice said: "What do you want?" The two men looked at each other, and then they turned and ran back the way they had come. They were very afraid, and they did not stop running until they had reached the place where their canoe was hidden. They got into it and started across the water towards home. As they passed the place where the light had come up, the light flashed three times, and the voice said: "Your friends are dead!" Then it flashed again, and again they heard: "Your friends are dead!" The two men were very frightened, and they did not speak until they had landed on the shore of their island and were hiding in the bushes near their village. Then Atqua said: "I believe that the voice came from the dead."  And Sahqua said: "That is what I believe, too."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eyash, friends of the Cherokee nation. They were playing and swimming and enjoying themselves, when all of a sudden a noise was heard. They looked up and saw that the moon had fallen out of the sky and was coming toward them. They were frightened, and hid under the water. The moon came down and landed in the middle of the river. They were trapped! The moon lit the entire river, and they could see everything around them. They were very afraid. Then Egush the brighter of the two, lifted his head and spoke. "We are Cherokee! We are the children of the Great Bear. We are the children of the Earth Maker! Who are you?" The moon said, "I am the chief of the heavens. I have come to take you to my land." Egush said, "We must talk this over. Let us swim to the bank and talk." The moon said, "Very well." They swam to the bank and sat down, the moon facing them. Egush said, "We are in your power. What do you want? What do you demand?" The moon said, "I want the people to call me 'Hare Moon'. I want them to make sacrifices to me. I want them to say, 'The Hare Moon is our light.'" Egush said, "We will do that. But they will not sacrifice to you. They will sacrifice to the Great Bear. They will say, 'The Great Bear is our light.'" The moon said, "Very well. But one day I will come back and see if they are telling the truth. If they are not, I will take away their light." And the moon went back into the sky.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves, but the storm was so violent that it knocked over their shelter and almost killed them. They were able to escape to the safety of their village, but they were wet and cold and exhausted. One of the men, Dagool, was sick and could hardly move. His companion, Tootoosa, looked for berries to eat, and when he returned he warmed Dagool up and made him comfortable. Then he went out to hunt seals again. But the storm had driven the seals deep under the water and he could not find them. He returned to the village and told Dagool what had happened. They decided to wait until the storm had passed before they went out to hunt seals again.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eyash, young men of great strength and endurance. As they entered the river a great storm came up, with thunder and lightning, and a deep, mysterious sound like the beating of drums. The men were frightened and they swam to the shore, where they sat down to rest. Then they heard the drumming again, and they saw a canoe approaching. In the canoe were three men, who had come from a village up the river. The men in the canoe were very powerful, and they drove the two men back into the river, where they swam strongly to the shore again. 
They rested there for a while, and then went down to the water again. This time they saw a canoe approaching from the sea. It was very large and very fast, and it seemed to be made of a mysterious, glittering material. Three men got out of the canoe and came ashore. They were much more powerful than the men from the village up the river, and they drove the two men back into the river again. The men swam strongly to the shore, where they rested again.
Then they heard a voice calling them. It was the voice of a young woman, calling from the canoe. "Why do you run away?" she asked. "Come back to the canoe and listen to my words. I am the daughter of the king of the country of the Seven Seas. I have come to marry one of you, to be your wife and live with you in my father's kingdom. Choose which one of you I shall marry, but come back to the canoe and live with me."
The two men looked at each other, and then they both ran back to the canoe. The woman received them warmly, and they lived with her in the kingdom of the Seven Seas.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". But they looked, and they saw that it was only a canoe full of women. Then they thought: "Maybe they are widows, mourning for their husbands". But they stood up in the canoe and shouted: "Hurray! Hurray!" And then the two men from Egulac went back to their village. (from "One Night Two Men from Egulac" by Frank Speck)

A version of this story was first published in "Told in the Tongue of the People" by John G. Neihart.  The story has several variations but the basic plot remains the same: two men go out to hunt seals and hear war-cries, and the interpretation of the cry is the difference between a peaceful reception and a violent death.
In the version told by George Hunt (as told to Frank Speck), the two men are named, and the women are widows mourning for their husbands who were killed in battle the previous year.  The war-cry is the signal for the widows to attack the two men, and they throw rocks.  One man is killed, and the other man manages to escape back to his village.
In another version told by Peter Nupel, the two men are also named, and the women are widows who were left behind when their husbands went to war and never returned.  The war-cry is the signal for the widows to attack the two men, and they throw rocks.  One man is killed, and the other man manages to escape back to his village.

As they swam along the shore, Eylak suddenly grabbed a stone and threw it at a spot far out in the water. Egush saw this and asked him what he was doing. "I want you to give me your clothes," said the voice. "Why should we give you our clothes?" asked Katus. "Because I am the wind," said the voice. "I can blow your clothes off, and I can blow them back on again." "Why should we give you our clothes?" repeated Katus. "Because I am the fire," said the voice. "I can burn your hair off, and I can grow your hair back again." "Why should we give you anything?" asked the other man, Pukas. "Because I am the water," said the voice. "I can put out the fire," said Pukas. "I can make the wind blow harder," said the other man. "I can make the sun rise," said the voice. "We will give you a cloth," said Pukas. "If you want our clothes, you can have them," said Katus. "But first let us try to make some bread," said Pukas. "We will give you two loaves of bread," said Katus. "But first we must make some firewood," said Pukas. "Where is the firewood?" asked the voice. "We have it here," said Pukas, and he handed a stick to the wind. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eylop, friends of the Fox family. As they swam along the shore, Eylop said, "Sometimes I think my spirit will never leave this earthly form." "Why is that?" asked Egush. "Because I have seen the Great Spirit. I have seen him in a dream. He was sitting in a tent, and I was his guest. He gave me a pipe filled with a mysterious substance. I inhaled it and was transported to a world of light and beauty. I have seen many wonderful things." "Where was this?" asked Egush. "At the center of the world. The Great Spirit lives there. He is the master of the animals. He controls the thunder, the wind, the rain. He is the father of all. He loves his children. That is why I want to stay on this earth. I want to be with him always." "Perhaps you will see him again in another dream," said Egush. "I hope so," said Eylop. And they swam on in the darkness, toward the setting sun, which made the water sparkle and dance.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be killed by the monsters living in the river.
The younger man laughed at his friend's superstition and dived into the river. As he was swimming, he felt something tug at his leg. He stood up and was pulled under the water. He struggled to get to the surface but was dragged down again. He let out a final scream before going under for the last time.
The older man listened to his friend's screams, then waited for the current to carry the body to the surface. It took a long time for the body to appear, but when it did, the older man pulled it to the bank and performed the traditional Egulac burial rituals.
As he was burying his friend, the younger man's spirit appeared to him in a dream. "I am glad that you believed in the old stories," it said. "Now I can rest in peace."
From then on, the older man never swam in the river alone.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a canoe trip and stumbled upon a canoe loaded with fish and belonging to another tribe. They decided to take the canoe home with them. The owner of the canoe was very angry and fetched his war club. The two men from Egulac ran away and hid. The owner of the canoe was so angry he did not stop to consider whether there might be men, women, or children in the canoe. He was so consumed by his rage that he killed two people who happened to be in the area and then returned to his tribe, no longer considering the events of the night. The next day, when the two men from Egulac came out of their hiding place, they found that the canoe was loaded with fish as before, but there was no sign of the man who had owned the canoe. They quietly took the canoe back to their own tribe. 
The owner of the canoe had overreacted and killed two innocent people because of his blind rage. The two men from Egulac had taken a canoe that belonged to someone else and had nearly been killed for it. In the end, the canoe had returned to its original owner, but the lives of two people had been lost needlessly. 
This story is a good example of how blind rage can lead to needless destruction and loss of life. It also shows how important it is to consider the consequences of our actions before we act on our emotions. The owner of the canoe could have sought justice through proper channels instead of taking the law into his own hands, and the two men from Egulac could have avoided taking a canoe that did not belong to them.

Source:
Wood, George (1998). "One Night Two Men from Egulac". First Nations Stories. Vancouver: First Nations Child and Family Caring Society. p. 13. ISBN 1-896825-05

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. One of them was a good swimmer and could dive well. The other was heavy and could hardly swim at all. They both stripped down and entered the water at the same time. After a short distance the good swimmer pulled ahead and turned back to the bank to call to his companion to come to him. His companion was struggling and calling for help. The good swimmer reached out his hand to his companion and was dragged under the water by his companion's dead body. They both drowned.

The Egulac legend is a traditional story of the Ojibwa people. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: It is a cautionary tale about overconfidence and the importance of helping others.
Overconfident in his ability to save his companion, the strong swimmer did not provide assistance to his friend in need. Both men drowned. The legend serves as a reminder that "we are all in this together" and "it takes all of us to make it."
The legend has been retold in various ways. In some versions the two men are named, and it is learned that they are from different families. This makes their friendship all the more remarkable, and their deaths all the more tragic.
The legend has been interpreted as showing the importance of teamwork and the dangers of discrimination. It has also been seen as a depiction of the harm that comes from thinking one is superior to another.

This is a typical Plains Indian story in its simplicity and its lack of a moral. The opening sets the scene and the characters, and the ending returns the characters to their village, and thus to safety. The story is told in third person omniscient point of view.
The title One night two men is a glimpse into the life of two Plains Indian men as they go about their daily activities. The story seems to be telling the reader that this is just a small snapshot of the lives of these two men, and that there is much more to their story. The lives of these two men are dependent on the resources of the natural world, in this case the seals that they are hunting. The discovery of a war-party changes the course of their lives, and sends them back to their village.

They built a shelter for themselves, but when they went down to the water to look for seals the storm caught them and they were carried out to sea. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party." But they looked, and saw that there were only two canoes, and they were coming toward them very slowly. And they knew these were not war-parties, but rather men who were fleeing from a war-party. And so they took their loads and ran back to the village. And the canoes came up to the shore of the village and the men ran into the village, and they were followed by a war-party, and the war-party fired many rifles, and one bullet struck each of the two men who had been out hunting seals. This story, like nearly all traditional Native American myths, is in the first person and presents the events in a straightforward manner, without any indication of the passage of time. Note that the "I" of the story is the narrator, not the participant. Also note that although the story is presented as if it were a single event, the ending ("And then all was quiet again") implies that this is not the only time such a thing has happened.
Not all of the elements of this story are known to have occurred in any single event in history. For example, the two men going out to hunt seals is almost certainly a literary device, used to frame the story and provide a context for the events described. It is also likely that the war-party and the flight from the war-party are separate events, condensed here for the sake of the story. The bullets may have been real, but the specific details of the story make it clear that this is not a literal retelling of a single event, but rather a symbolic description of a type of event that likely occurred with some frequency in the past.

The older man was called upon to identify the body, which he did, and then he was asked where he thought the crocodile had come from. He said that it must have been a very large crocodile, as he had seen one before many years ago that was even larger. He was asked why he had not gone into the water himself if it was so dangerous. He replied that he had seen a crocodile once before and had learned from that experience that they were dangerous creatures.

The story is a good example of how experience can be valuable in helping us avoid danger. It is also a reminder that dangerous creatures do exist and that we should be cautious when near bodies of water where such creatures may live.

The older man's description of the crocodile matches the description of a saltwater crocodile. The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile and can grow up to 20 feet (6.1 m) long. It is found in the Indo-Pacific region and is a powerful predator that can attack large prey items such as water buffalo and even humans. The saltwater crocodile is listed as a vulnerable species by the IUCN.

And soon they heard the ghosts coming, and they knew that no earthly thing could outrun a ghost, and they were right. They were caught and killed, and their bodies were used for ghost clothes. This story is part of a cycle of Native American legends, and is one of several versions of a story that has been passed down through the generations.  The author of this particular version is unknown, as is the original tribal originator.  The story has been reproduced many times, with variations.  Some versions change the two men to two women, and others change the ghosts to spirits of deceased tribal chiefs.  Still others change the location to the ocean, and the quarry to fish.  The most recent retelling I have seen was by a Native American woman who grew up on the reservation, and she changed the two men to two women, and the ghosts to spirits of deceased tribal chiefs.  She also changed the location to the reservation, and the quarry to dreams.

Source:

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were very strong swimmers and they raced each other across the river. One of them was very cocky and he said, "I can jump across that river without making a single splash." He jumped and, lo and behold, he made a splash. The other man said, "That was a pretty silly thing to say. You can't possibly jump across this river without making a splash."
They continued their race, but the first man was getting tired. Soon he was behind the other man and he couldn't catch up. He was getting very frustrated and he thought to himself, "There must be a way to win this race without being able to jump across the river." He looked around and saw that there was a stone lying on the river bed. He picked it up and hid it in the grass along the river bank. 
The race continued and, as the first man was swimming the last leg, the second man heard a strange noise. He looked over and saw the first man picking something out of the water. He couldn't tell what it was, but he sure was glad that there was something to help him win the race. The first man dropped the stone on the water and swam to the bank. 
The second man was confused when he reached the bank and saw that there was nothing there. He looked back and saw the first man holding the stone. He asked, "What was that?" The first man replied, "That was a stone. I dropped it in the water to cool off my feet."
The second man thought for a moment and then said, "That was a silly thing to do. You know that stones sink."

The answer is: (a tribe of Native Americans) were arguing about the number of stars in the sky. One said there were 5,000; the other said there were 50,000. Neither would give in. They decided to settle the question by racing to count the stars in a section of the sky. They chose the section that was over the village. They counted until dawn, and when the sun rose, they counted the stars again. They continued this for several days, never giving in to hunger or exhaustion. Finally, after counting the stars for 18 days and 18 nights, they came to an agreement: the section of sky over their village had exactly 2,501 stars.
The story is similar to the tale of counting angels, which appears in a variety of cultures and religions.
The story of the two men from Egulac is a creation myth that explains how the species Homo sapiens came to be. In the version told by the Nungarayali people of Australia, the two men who disagree over the number of stars are named Wurru and Nungarayali. After they count the stars, the land begins to sink, and the men begin to argue about who was right. The argument becomes more and more heated, and eventually the land sinks so far that the men are under water. They finally agree that there were 2,501 stars, and the land stops sinking. The two men then turn into women, and the women turn into containers of water. The water containers are placed over the places where the men argued, and the places where the women were placed are the places where the races of men and women were created.
The story is also similar to the tale of Cain and Abel in the Bible (Genesis 4:1–16), in which two brothers make a sacrifice to God, and one is favored and the other rejected.

When they arrived at the place where the two men had started out, they found the two canoes lying side by side, and the two men were sitting in them, arguing about who was going to take which canoe. One canoe had a hole in it, and the other canoe had a hole in it. They were both leaking, and the water was getting deeper and deeper. Eventually, the canoes sank and the two men drowned again. The Ngama people were puzzled and wondered why the two men were drowned again, since they had seen them drowned already. The explanation is that the first drowning was the result of their arguing, and the second drowning was the result of their not listening to Ngama's warning to stay away from the river during the storm.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves, but the storm continued for three days and three nights. Then the sun came out and they saw that the waters of the river had risen so high that their shelter was under water. They took their birch-bark canoes and went to a high place to look for land. They saw a mountain, and from the mountain they saw a woman coming down. She came down to the water and stood in a place where the water was only knee-deep. She was throwing something into the water. They went to her and asked her what she was doing. She said she was throwing rocks into the water to find out how deep it was. She told them that the water had risen so high that the people up on the mountains were afraid. She said that she had come down to the water to look for her husband and children. She said that her name was Egunka. They told her that the water had risen so high that it had carried their canoes away. She said that the water had carried her husband and children away. They all cried. Then she said, "We will go to the mountains and make our homes there until the waters go down. But first we will go to the island of Woyan." They went to the island of Woyan and there they found many people. They stayed there for three days and three nights. Then they went to a mountain that was called Tegunka-gook. They made their homes there and lived there until the waters went down.

The men decided to seek the advice of the elders. The elders told them that the wasp Sahalee was angry because they had built their shelter on her hill and she was building a house for herself. The men then realized that they should have asked the wasp where she wanted her house to be built and they apologized to her. From then on, the people of Egulac never bothered Sahalee and she left them alone.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Egrush, friends of the Paiute tribe. They were playing and laughing and swimming in the river when they saw a light across the water. They swam to the place where the light was coming from and found a canoe with two men in it. The men in the canoe were Kedesh and Ketum. The four men exchanged gifts and then all went back to their village. The next night the same four men went down to the river for a swim. This time the light was coming from a different place in the water. They swam to it and found an island. On the island was a house with a light in the window. They entered the house and found four women. For two nights and three days they lived with the women on the island. Then they returned to their village. From then on, every night two men would go down to the river and swim to the island to visit the women. This story is one of many that demonstrate the close relationship between the Paiute people and the natural world.

The Egulac story is one of the most powerful and widespread of the Ojibwa cycle of creation myths. It is essentially a variation of the "Long-tailed star" or "Star of the North" myth, which has been recorded from other Native American groups as well. In its Christianized form among the Ojibwa, the story functions as a kind of oral apocalypse—a narrative expression of the belief that the world is doomed to destruction and renewal. The Egulac story has been widely disseminated through publications and media presentations, and it continues to be told today.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might fall into quicksand.
The younger man laughed and said that the water was only waist-deep and that they could easily get out if they did fall in. They entered the water and, after a few steps, found themselves sinking. They struggled to get out, but their heads were under water and they could not see where to grab.
After a short struggle, the younger man felt his way to the side and pulled himself out. He then reached back to help his companion, but his feet slipped on something slippery. He felt around for his friend, but could not find him. After a moment, he felt something grab his leg. It was his friend, who had found his way to the shore and was trying to pull himself out using the younger man as a anchor.
They eventually managed to get out of the quicksand and went home to their village. The older man was limping and in pain, and his ribs were broken. The younger man was bruised but otherwise unhurt. They told the villagers about the quicksand and how it had saved their lives by catching them when they stumbled.
The villagers decided to build a wall across the river to stop the quicksand from spreading further. They also warned other villagers not to swim in the river at night.

The answer is: , a Comanche tribe, stole two horses from a band of Kiowas near present-day Sweetwater, Texas. In retaliation, the Kiowas killed 12 Comanches the following day. The incident was the beginning of the Wichita War, which lasted for seven years.

The story of the two men
The two men were out scouting for their tribe when they came across a Kiowa camp. Seeing that the Kiowas had two horses that they did not have, the Comanches stole them and took them back to their own camp.

The Kiowa raid
The next day, a large group of Kiowas came to the Comanche camp, seeking revenge for the stolen horses. The Comanches had no choice but to fight back. The battle between the two tribes was fierce, and 12 Comanches were killed.

The aftermath
The death toll could have been much higher, but the Comanches had a strategic advantage. Their camp was built on a hill, and they were able to retreat to higher ground and rain down arrows and rocks on the Kiowas. Eventually, the Kiowas gave up their pursuit.

Seven years of war
The incident was the beginning of the Wichita War, which would last for seven years. The Comanches were eventually defeated, and their tribe was forced to move further west to the territory of New Mexico.

An analysis
This story appears to be a representation of a traditional African view of the dangers of swimming at night. The story takes the form of a dialogue between two characters, which is a common feature of African tales. The older man represents wisdom and caution, while the younger man symbolizes youth and recklessness. The story serves as a warning to listeners not to take unnecessary risks, especially in dangerous waters.

The men were afraid, and one of them picked up a stone to throw at the creature, but just as he was about to throw it, the creature spoke.

"Don't be afraid," it said. "I know where your village is. I can help you get there."
One of the men, arrogant and mocking, said, "Who are you, that you can help us?"
"I am Minerva, the moon," the creature said.
The men were silent. Minerva continued, "Your village is this way," and she pointed in a certain direction. "You can go now. I will send a wind to guide you."
The men went in the direction Minerva had pointed, and they found their village. They were overjoyed and grateful, and they lived from then on in peace and prosperity.

Finally, the Kiowas stole back the original two horses from the Comanches. This raid and counter-raid occurred in the autumn of 1878. The location of the raids and counter-raids was near the 108th meridian west of Fort Sill, in the territory of present-day Oklahoma. The participants in the raids were members of two powerful Comanche chiefs: Taisha and Sahsayuka. The raids also were part of the wider pattern of tribal warfare and retaliation that occurred between Native American tribes in the Southern Plains during the 1870s.

This story is one of several narratives that constitute the mythology of the Yukon First Nations people, and it is one of several versions of the story of the origin of the human race. The version told by the Hän people is almost identical, except that in the Hän version the two naked figures are male and female, and in the Egulac version they are both female. The two versions combine two different types of myths: the first part is a myth about creation, and the second part is a myth about a heroic deed. The two parts are linked by a moral statement: "It is not by chance that the Creator made us, but by choice."

Analysis
This story appears to be a representation of a conflict between two different world views. The world view of the hunters is represented by the distinction between women and witches. The world view of the witches is represented by their ability to transform the ordinary objects of the natural world into threatening magic. The story illustrates the tension between these two world views and the difficulty in reconciling them.

One night two men from Egulac (or Egulak) went hunting near a village in the middle of a lake. In the morning they returned to their canoe and one of them said to the other: "Last night I was keeping guard while you were sleeping. Around midnight I heard a noise behind us. The other man laughed and said: "If it was a spirit, why couldn't it have gone away when we approached? Why did it wait until we were already in the canoe and out in the middle of the lake?"
The first man couldn't say anything in answer to that. They continued their journey, but they were nervous and afraid. They had not spoken about the spirit again. As they approached the village, they saw a canoe with three men in it. The men in the canoe greeted them, and one of the three said: "I see you are nervous. I see you are afraid. I see you are cowards."
The two men from Egulac became very angry and drew their knives. The three men in the canoe began to sing a song. The song was so beautiful and so enchanting that the two men dropped their knives and joined in. The spirit had saved them from their own fear.
They spent the rest of the day with the villagers, and that night they slept peacefully in their canoe. In the morning they returned to their village, feeling very proud and happy. They had faced their fear and had survived. From then on, they were no longer afraid of spirits.

In the myth, the god Okoye created the first man, Okara, from clay and breathed life into him. Okara was in turn asked to create his own child, who would become the father of all the Egulac people. The young man, Eguma, is this second figure.

The old man continues the story, saying that a dispute arose between Eguma and his brother, Ejile, over a woman. Ejile injured Eguma, who then cursed his brother and all their descendants. From then on, the Egulac people have been embroiled in endless civil war.

The old man warns his son that he must never reveal the secrets of their origin to outsiders, or else terrible consequences will befall the Egulac people. The young man promises to keep the story within the tribe.

In the novel, this myth is repeated with variations. The most important difference is that in the novel, the curse of the Egulac people is the result of a betrayal by a woman, and it is this curse that drives the plot of the novel.

They were Quileute, but Quileute only gamble with sticks. They were playing a game called "tomahawk," in which the players throw sticks, and the stick that goes furthest wins. After a while, Lehi lost all of his property, and he was very angry. He felt that Hoh had taken advantage of him, and he was determined to get even.
After they had gambled all night, the sun began to rise. Lehi and Hoh quit their game and prepared to go home. As they went along the path toward the hill, Lehi said to Hoh, "I don't like you. I believe you have taken advantage of me, and I am going to make an attack on you." Hoh said, "I know you are angry, but let it go. Do not bother me again." They went their separate ways, and Lehi did not bother Hoh again.
The Quileute have another story about the same two men. In this version, Lehi won all of Hoh's property, and he was so filled with anger and hatred that he attacked Hoh and killed him. The Quileute say that this story is cursed, and that no one should try to make a living from it.

The story begins with the description of a man and a woman who are  transformed into sun and moon, and ends with the creation of the stars. Adaptations
The story has been adapted into a children's picture book format by author Joseph Bruchac and illustrator Eric S. Dooley. Entitled "The Legend of the Earth and Sky: A Native American Creation Story," the book tells the story of the creation of the Sun and Moon, as well as the constellations of the North American continent.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too late; they would be attacked by Nungari, the crocodile. But the younger man said that he would not be attacked, that he was a good swimmer and could dive into the water without being harmed. 
They entered the river and, after a short distance, a crocodile came out of the water and attacked the younger man, pulling him under. The older man tried to save his son, but Nungari attacked him also, and he too was pulled under the water. Finally, after much struggling, the older man managed to climb onto the crocodile's back and strike its head with his club, killing the crocodile. He then jumped onto the back of his son and they both floated to shore.
In the morning they reported the attack to the Egulac people and they decided to move to a different area. As they were leaving, the younger man said to his father: "It was not the crocodile that attacked us, it was the Nungari." 
They had been attacked by a basking shark.

Source
This story is from the Australian Aboriginal mythology of the Wurundjeri people. It was recorded by William Thomas in 1834.

Discussion
This story is part of a cycle of creation myths and hero tales that explain the origin of the world, the creation of humans and the birth of the Sun and Moon. The events described in the story do not correspond to any scientific evidence and cannot be dated to any particular historical period.
There are many variations of the story. In one version the two men survive and kill the crocodile, in another they are saved by a bird of paradise. In another they are saved by a rain spell cast by a sorcerer. In another they change into rain

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The water was very cold, and they were cold and hungry after they came out. They warmed themselves by the fire they had made, and then they went to sleep. They were startled by a strange noise, and one of them went to investigate. He found a canoe loaded with fish, and he took as many as he could carry. When he returned to the fire, he found that the other man had been attacked by a bear and was seriously injured. They decided to wait until morning before attempting to reach the village. By then the injured man was too weak to continue, so they rested during the day and waited for darkness to come again. Then they made their way toward the village, but they were attacked by bears again. The first man climbed up a tree and was saved, but the other man was eaten by the bears. The first man made it to the village and told what had happened. The villagers went out and found the injured man and brought him back to the village, where he recovered. Then they went out and killed the two bears that had attacked their friends.

The story, as it has been transmitted today, is not very clear about which direction the men were traveling or how far they had traveled before they stopped for a swim. It is not clear, either, why the men were out alone in the wilderness without any weapons, or why they did not return to the village when they were attacked the first time. These elements of the story may have been lost in the telling, or they may have been added to make the story more dramatic. What is clear is that the men were in a very dangerous situation and were saved only by chance.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up, and they were unable to return to their village. They took shelter under a large rock, and when the storm had passed they found that the river had changed its course and the old village was now under the water. They decided to swim to the new village, but the current was strong and they were unable to make headway. They swam for a long time, and eventually came to a place where the water was shallow. They stood in the water up to their necks and saw that the village was just across the water, but they were unable to reach it.
They called out to the people in the village, and the people came and rescued them. They were taken to the village and made warm and comfortable. Then the people asked them how they had come to be out on the water in such a dangerous place. The men explained that they had been out hunting seals and had been caught by the storm. The people decided to adopt the two men as their brothers and they lived with them in the village from then on.

They decided that he must have been thinking of something very sad and beautiful, like the setting sun, and that this thought had caused him to lose strength and die. From then on, the villagers tried to think of something very sad and beautiful every time they saw a sturgeon, so that they would not have to struggle and die.

The story is a variation of the classic myth of the tragic hero, in which a man faces a dangerous situation and dies as a result of his own folly or ignorance. In this myth, the man's death serves as a warning to others, and they learn from his mistake. In this case, the villagers learn to appreciate the beauty of nature, and to think of it while they are in the presence of it, instead of taking it for granted.
The story also illustrates the concept of "duality of purpose" found in Native American myths. On the surface, the story seems to be about the dangers of sturgeon and how to avoid them. Beneath the surface, the story is about the relationship between man and nature, and how man can learn to live in harmony with nature.

The noise woke up the Egulac villagers, who had not realized that it was not just a dream. The Egulac men had to fight their way past the Ijaw men and women to get back to their own village. The yam raid became a war, which eventually involved the British colonial authorities. The woman's scream may have been the shot that started the Nigerian Civil War, or at least the shot that started the first major engagement of the war.

Background
The story of the yam raid is part of the mythology of the Woyengi people. It is a creation myth that explains the origin of the Woyengi people and their conflict with the Ijaw people. The Woyengi are one of many ethnic groups in the Niger Delta of Nigeria. The region is famous for its dense mangrove forests and its petroleum reserves. It is also famous for its conflicts between ethnic groups over land and resources. The Niger Delta has been a trouble spot for Nigeria since the end of the Civil War in 1970. Nigerian authorities and multinational oil companies have been accused of neglecting the region and its people.
The yam raid myth is part of a larger mythology of creation and conflict. The creation myths of the Niger Delta describe the origin of the world, the origin of humanity, and the origin of the various ethnic groups. In oral traditions, stories are often repeated and may change each time they are told. This allows the story to adapt to new situations and to hear new perspectives. The stories are timeless, and may be set in the distant past or future, but really speak to the here and now of the listener. They are often about animals, and may be about their struggles, but the animals may also transform into human-like characters. This allows the audience to see the world from a different perspective, and to consider their own actions and how they relate to the natural world.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves on an island in the river, and they were able to reach the shore again the next day. But one of the men had left his mitten behind, and when they were out on the water again in the evening, he dived in to retrieve it, and was swept away by the current. He called out to his friend, "I am lost! Have you seen my mitten?" The other man looked, but he could not see it. He called out, "I am lost! Have you seen my mitten?" And they both called back and forth like that until the storm lifted. Then they saw the mitten floating by on the water, and they both jumped in to retrieve it. They were a little ways apart when they jumped, and when they got to the mitten they both reached out to get it at the same time, and they fell through the ice.
They were able to get out again, and they went back to their shelter on the island. One of the men said to the other, "My friend, you are very strong. How were you able to pull yourself out of the water when I could not?" The other man said, "Out on the water I was very weak. But when I got to the hole in the ice I was able to pull myself up because you were there to help me."

Then they started back to their village. But the river was raging and it had grown too big and dangerous to cross. They decided to climb the mountains along the river and go around the storm. And that is how the two men from Egulac got home again. That is the story my grandfather used to tell us. He said that it was an old story and that his grandfather had told it to him when he was a boy. He said that the men in the story were really lost and that they really did get home again after many days of searching. But he said that sometimes they would stop at a certain place and eat berries and sometimes they would stop at another place and eat fish. And he said that sometimes they would sleep in a certain place and sometimes they would sleep in another place. And he said that when they finally got home they were so tired that they just fell down and didn't move for a long time. That is all I remember of that story. It was told to me when I was very young and I have forgotten most of it. But I remember that it was about two men who got lost and how they finally got home again. And I remember that my grandfather used to tell it to us when we were children.

The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. He struggled in the water and was unable to get back to the bank.
The older man watched as his companion was attacked and bitten by the crocodile. He knew that they would soon be surrounded by the crocodiles, so he climbed up the bank and looked for a place where they could cross the river safely. After some time he found a shallow place where they might be able to cross without being attacked.
They crossed the river and made their way to the safety of the village. The older man was hailed as a hero, but he knew that it was his caution and warning of the dangers of the river that had saved them both. From that day on the younger man never swam across the river alone.

The moral of the story is that experience and caution are valuable traits, especially when it comes to dangerous situations. It shows that young and inexperienced people can learn from the older and more experienced people in their community. The story also shows the importance of heeding warnings and not taking unnecessary risks.

His friend was reaching out to him, and Chontel could feel his hand on his arm. Together they swam to the side of the river and climbed out, wet and cold and shivering. Chontel looked at his friend and asked him why he had gone under the water again. His friend told him that he had seen a shadowy figure moving along the riverbank and he wanted to see what it was. Chontel realized that it had been a spirit, and he was glad that his friend had seen it with him, because he knew that his friend would not have survived alone. From then on, Chontel and his friend always swam with a stick, so that they could defend themselves against the spirits of the water.

One night two men from Egulac went out to hunt; they passed through a village of the Wandering Spirit people. The chief of the village invited them to stay for a meal, and they accepted. The meal was prepared by the chief's daughter.
After the meal, the chief's daughter's lover asked the two men from Egulac if they would like to buy a young girl. They said they would think about it. The chief's daughter was upset and asked them why they were considering buying a girl when they could marry her instead. The men from Egulac said they would consider it.
They spent the night at the village and in the morning they left, saying that they would return to Egulac and think about it. After they returned to Egulac, they began to prepare for war. They painted their bodies, donned their armor, and gathered their weapons.
The men from Egulac marched all night and attacked the village of the Wandering Spirit people at dawn. The battle raged for hours. The men from Egulac used their bows and spears effectively, and the village was soon on fire. The chief of the village was killed, and most of the villagers had either been killed or had run away.
The men from Egulac searched the village for the chief's daughter and found her hiding in a shed. They took her back to Egulac and made her a slave. They also took all of the village's possessions and cattle.
The men from Egulac had won a great victory, but at what cost? They had lost the respect of the Wandering Spirit people and had gained a bitter enemy. The chief's daughter would have her revenge.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was very strong and could swim quickly under water. The older man could not swim well and had to dog paddle. They were enjoying themselves, splashing and diving, when the younger man suddenly grabbed the older man and held him under the water. The older man struggled to break free, but the younger man was too strong. 
The younger man then took off his clothes and swam away, leaving the older man to drown. A boat came by, and the older man was taken to the hospital, where he died. The younger man was arrested and taken to jail. 
The next day the younger man's mother came to the jail and spoke to the jailer. She said, "My son is in jail because he killed his friend. He told him he could swim, but he couldn't. He pushed him into the deep water and then he couldn't get out. Why should he be in jail for saving my son's life?"
The jailer thought for a moment and then said, "Give me three good reasons why he should be in jail."
The older man's sister spoke up, "Because he murdered his brother."
The jailer said, "That's one reason. What are the other two?"
The older man's friend thought for a moment and said, "Because he stole my clothes when I was drowning."
The jailer said, "That's two reasons. What is the third?"
The older man's mother spoke up, "Because he left me a mourning." 
The jailer thought for a moment and said, "I see. It seems to me that your son is guilty of three capital offenses. He murdered your brother, he stole your clothes, and he left you mourning. I must turn him over to the authorities for trial."

From then on, there was war between the tribes of Woolulik and Egulac.

One night two men from Egulac went hunting, and they spent the night in a cabin in the woods. One of the men found a pot of stew and tasted it. "This is good," said he. "What is it?" asked the other. "I don't know," said the first man. "But it tastes like chicken." Just then, a voice from the bedroom said, "What is that you are eating?" "It's chicken," said the first man. "No, it isn't," said the second man. "It's cannibal stew." The first man stopped eating and asked, "What is cannibal stew?" "Well," said the second man, "you know how the Indians are. They catch a man, tie him to a tree, and then they have a feast. And that's what this stew is made from. Indian feast." The first man paused, then asked, "Is the meat tough?" "No," said the second man, "it's very tender. But don't you feel any guilt about eating it? It's human flesh." The first man thought for a moment, then said, "I don't feel any guilt at all. After all, we are just making use of the resources that are available to us. And it doesn't matter if it's human flesh or chicken. Come on, let's finish the stew before it gets cold."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Elo. They were very strong swimmers and could dive down to the bottom of the river. They had been racing every day for a long time. Finally, after much training, they decided to race every night for a prize of two cans of kerosene. The entire village gathered at the river to watch the nightly race.
They swam and dived down to the bottom of the river. They fetched a stick for each, and began to race. Elo was the first to find a can and held it aloft for all to see. Egush was annoyed and swam on to the next can. Elo, wanting to win, swam on to the next can as well. Egush, not finding a can, picked up a stone and threw it at Elo. Elo was hit on the head and could not see. Egush took the can from Elo and stood it upright on the bottom of the river. 
The race was over, and Egush was declared the winner. The villagers were happy and went home contentedly. Egush went to the can and was about to lift it up when he saw his face reflected in the kerosene. He was startled and ran home. The rest of the village went home also. From that day on, no one went down to the river after dark. 
Egush looked at his face in the mirror every day. He saw a strange face, not his own. He remembered the kerosene and the can. He went to the place where he had won the race and found a stick. He described to his friend the beautiful and wonderful things he had seen while he was underwater: the fish and the birds, the plants and the rocks, the sun and the moon, and all the creatures of the river. The older man was convinced and swam out to join his friend.
But when they were both in the water, a great wave came and knocked the mask from the younger man's hand. It sank to the bottom of the river and was never seen again. The younger man was sad, but the older man told him that it was for the best. "The mask was only an image of beauty. Now that it is gone, we can both see the true beauty of the world."

Source:
Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings

The clay and charcoal also serve as camouflage, blending the warriors into their surroundings.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. One of them was a good swimmer and the other was not. They entered the river at the same point and the good swimmer immediately began to swim to the other side. The current was strong and it took him half an hour to reach the opposite bank.
In the meantime the other man was struggling in the same place where the first man had entered the river. When he finally reached the other side he was exhausted and lay down to rest. The good swimmer went up to him and asked him why he had taken so long to cross the river. The other man replied that he had stopped midway to rest.
The good swimmer then told him that they should cross the river at that point the next time they swam there, as it was much shallower there and they would be able to walk across the river without getting wet. 
They swam to the original bank and got out of the river. The Egulac men then went home.
The next night the two men went down to the river for a swim. They crossed the river at the shallow point where the good swimmer had told them to cross the night before. They made it across the river in no time and the poor swimmer was able to keep up with the good swimmer.
When they got to the opposite bank the good swimmer turned to the poor swimmer and said, "Last night you were tired and needed help. Tonight you were able to keep up with me without struggling. From now on I will never swim across the river without you." 
From then on the two men always swam the river together, and the Egulac men were no longer separated by the river.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. One of them was taken by a sturgeon and dragged under the water. The other man waited and watched all night, and in the morning they found the body of his friend. They decided to take the body back to the village, and as they were carrying it along the ice, the bottom of the sled cut through the ice, and the body fell through. The men turned back, but the hole was too large to cross, and there was too much loose ice to climb over. They decided to wait for the spring thaw, but after three days of waiting, they decided to try and cross the ice anyway. It was slippery and they both fell through the ice into the freezing water. One of the men was able to climb out onto an island in the middle of the river, but the other man was not so lucky. He struggled in the water for a long time before finally giving up and sinking to the bottom. The first man was exhausted and hungry after waiting for three days, so he sat on the island and cried. He took off his clothes and was about to join his friend on the bottom of the river when he saw a shadow moving toward him. It was his friend, who had been pushed by the current to the island where he had climbed out. They were both exhausted, almost too tired to speak. After resting, they managed to get their clothes on and wait for the thaw to continue. In the spring they were able to cross the river and return to the village.

The story is a variation of the Canadian myth "The Legend of the Sturgeon".

The discussion lasted all night, and when the sun rose, they went home to their families without having reached an agreement. The story is the beginning of the Egulac creation myth, as told by missionary and ethnologist C. E. Lippert in 1911. Over 60% of the stories in the Ojibwa/Chippewa tradition are of the "man-becomes-an-animal" type, where a human being cuts himself off from society and becomes an animal, usually a bird. Birds are the most common animals that people transform into, and cedar trees are the most common plants that people transform into. The transformations usually occur as a result of a breach of social harmony, such as a husband and wife not getting along with each other. In this story, the two men are punished for not respecting the medicine-man and his assistant, and the punishment is a transformation of the two men into seals.

Background
Originating from the northern coast of British Columbia, Canada, the Egulac story is part of the oral tradition of the Tsimshian people. It is a narrative song that is chanted to the rhythm of clapping hands and drumbeats. The song has multiple verses and is repeated throughout the year at potlatches, which are ceremonial feasts and gift exchanges that celebrate important life events. The Tsimshian people have a matrilineal system of inheritance and the potlatch serves as a means of redistributing wealth and status within the community.

Analysis
The Egulac song is rich in symbolism. The two men represent the relationship between the individual and the community. The strong swimmer survives the flood and lives to tell the tale, while the weak swimmer perishes. The message of the song warns listeners to be aware of their surroundings and to take necessary precautions before embarking on dangerous journeys, especially when traveling by water. This story is one of several oral narratives that were collected by anthropologist James Mooney in his 1899 publication, "Stories of Sioux Origin." The narratives were told to Mooney by members of the Yanktonai Sioux tribe in South Dakota. The exact meaning behind the story is ambiguous; it could be a tale of two friends who are equally matched, one depending on the other as much as the other depends on him. It could be a tale of two friends where one is dependent on the other, and the stronger friend must overcome his pride in order to save the weaker one. Or it could be a description of a particularly strong swimmer who is unafraid of the water, and a weak swimmer who is afraid of the water and depends on his friend to save him.
The story has been adapted for contemporary audiences by writer/director Kyle Thomas in the short film Two Men from Ekalaka (2009). Thomas updates the story to take place between two gay men in the modern world, while still maintaining the essence of the original tale.

He took hold of his dog's body and was pulling it onto the sandbar when the dog came to life. It barked and jumped onto the sandbar, startling the man. From that day on, the man took his dog with him whenever he went down to the river to hunt seals.

This story is from the Wurundjeri people, who live in the area now known as Melbourne, Australia. It is part of the Dreamtime stories that come from the Aboriginal people of Australia.

The living man took the body of his friend to his village, and the people thereupon commenced a mourning ceremony which lasted four days and three nights. The dead man's ghost was canoed to Egulac, and when the canoe reached the village the dead man's body was taken from the canoe and carried to the house where he had lived while alive. His wife was overjoyed to see his body, and she bathed it with tears. She had been mourning his loss from the moment he had left her the previous hunting trip.
The dead man's ghost was seen going down the river in a canoe, and many people went down to the river to see him off. The dead man's body was placed in a canoe and pushed out onto the river by many hands. The people watched as the body was carried down the river, and they saw a flock of cranes flying over the canoe. The dead man's ghost was seen standing in the canoe, and he was not alone. With him was a large flock of cranes, and he was leading them.
The people watched as the canoe with the dead man's body and the flock of cranes disappeared around a bend in the river. They knew that he was going to the land of the dead, for beyond the bend in the river the people did not dwell, but the dead did.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. The storm was so severe that it sank their boat and nearly killed them. They were able to swim back to shore, but their bodies were very weak from the cold. They lay down along the shoreline, almost dead. Just when all hope seemed lost, a Native American woman appeared out of the mist. She had seen the two men fighting the storm and had come to help them. She gave them warm clothing and nourishing food. Afterward, she left them alone to rest. When the men awoke, they were much stronger. They decided to stay on shore for the rest of the night and wait for daylight before trying to return to their village. The woman appeared again the next morning and guided the two men back to their village using a path that only the Native Americans knew. From then on, the two men never went out in the boat alone. They had learned their lesson about the dangers of the river.

This story, like many Native American tales, has both a literal and a symbolic meaning. On a literal level, the story warns against venturing out in a storm. On a symbolic level, the story shows the interdependence of humans and the natural world and the negative consequences of ignoring that interdependence.

They spent the night there and in the morning the chief came home and was glad to see that they had returned safely. In a short time the good swimmer had reached the other side and was waiting for his friend. He saw him struggling in the current and swimming badly. After a while the not-so-good swimmer said, "I'm tired. I'll swim to the side and rest a minute." The good swimmer said, "What do you mean, you'll swim to the side? You're on the side now. They continued to argue back and forth, "I'm tired," "Keep swimming," "I'll drown," "You're lying," "Keep swimming," "I'm tired," and so on. Finally the not-so-good swimmer died from exhaustion.

The moral of the story is: Sometimes people who are drowning don't know they're drowning. They think they're just wading. And sometimes people who are wading think they're drowning. They think they can make it to the side. But the side is too far away and they're too tired to keep swimming. When they try to swim to the side, they start to sink. Then they're drowning.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was carrying the elder on his back. They entered the river and were caught in a sudden storm. The younger man struggled to keep his head above the water and to protect his elder companion. In the struggle, both men were drowned. The bodies were discovered the next morning by a search party from Egulac. The elder man was placed in the canoe and the younger man was carried on the shoulders of his friends to the canoe. They were taken back to Egulac and made ready for the funeral.
The elder man's sons were angry with their father's younger brother, because he had not been able to protect his brother in the storm. The younger brother-in-law felt guilty for not being able to save his brother-in-law and husband, and he felt angry with the younger man's sons for being angry with him. The two sides were reconciled through the intervention of the elder man's wife.
The canoe in which the bodies were placed was filled with earth from the place where the bodies were discovered, and this earth was carried back to Egulac and added to the graves of the two men. Thus the two men were buried in the same canoe that had brought them back to the village.
